newsitem.title: USA: Cuban-born bankers convicted of fraud in New York.
newsitem.headline: Cuban-born bankers convicted of fraud in New York.

text.p: A New York jury found Cuban-born businessman Orlando Castro Llanes guilty on Wednesday of defrauding Venezuelan depositors of millions of dollars through a Puerto Rican bank.

His son, Orlando Castro Castro, 47, and his grandson, Jorge Castro Barredo, 29, were also found guilty of fraud and grand larceny in the case, where jurors also had to decide a key issue of whether New York had jurisdiction.
The elder Castro, 71, faces up to four years in prison. His son could be jailed for up to 25 years and his grandson up to 40 years. The judge scheduled sentencing for March 20.
Castro Llanes' attorney, Richard Sharpstein, said he would appeal the verdict. "This is literally going to be the 'Star Wars' of jurisdiction as it exists now in foreign banking cases."

Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau had argued that millions of dollars were fraudulently transferred through New York banks. The defence claimed no one in New York was defrauded and that Morgenthau overstepped his bounds.
The eldest Castro and his son also face six arrest warrants in Venezuela on financial fraud charges. The youngest is wanted in the Dominican Republic.

Prosecutors said the three men illegally used deposits in a family-controlled bank in Puerto Rico, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR), to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.
BPIPR closed in January 1995, with uninsured losses to depositors of more than $15 million.
Prosecutors say the three bankers had misled Venezuelan depositors into believing BPIPR was a safe offshore bank, subject to tight regulatory control, and attracted deposits of more than $55 million.
Prosecutors also claimed the defendants lied to regulators in Puerto Rico by falsely claiming BPIPR funds were held in Panama and thus not subject to Puerto Rican oversight.

Defence attorneys claimed the charges are the result of a desire for revenge by the Venezuelan government. Castro, a Cuban exile accused of playing a key role in Venezuela's 1994 banking crisis, left Venezuela that year after arrest warrants were issued for him and several associates on charges of financial fraud and other crimes.
He, his son and his grandson have been in jail since being arrested last April in Florida.

Shortly before the jury reached their verdict, the panel asked the judge if they were "bound to follow the law, even if we disagree with it when it comes to jurisdiction of the case." The judge replied that they were.

One of the 12 jurors, who listened to 44 witnesses and pored over 400 exhibits during the 4-month-long trial, said initially seven or eight members of the panel had doubts about the jurisdiction issue. But he said that a $500,000 check paid out by Citibank in New York was important evidence.

"It doesn't matter that the checks were drawn in Venezuela ... the fact is they were paid here in New York City and dollars were obtained here," said the juror, 30-year-old computer operator Bryan Cooper. The jury deliberated for nine hours over two days.
